## SCENE 02: Why It Spreads
image: s02_marching_crowd
prompt: Doug stands off to one side with one eyebrow raised, watching a long line of tiny doodle people staring at phones and marching toward a giant calendar with a single flag planted on the first day. Plain white background, 16:9.

### Narration
(smug) {cam:pan_left|6} {text:THE CLAIM|slam} Internet claim: everyone's doing it, so it must be a great idea.
(flat) [pause] {text:REALITY CHECK|pop} Reality check. It probably spreads for reasons that have nothing to do with results.
(deadpan) {sfx:whoosh} First, it has a start date. {text:FRESH START|jitter} Researchers call the reset feeling "the fresh start effect."
{cam:zoom_in|6} People tend to chase goals more after dates that feel like a clean slate, like Mondays, birthdays, or new months.
(smug) {sfx:pop} November first is basically {text:MONDAY|pop} Monday in a coat. [pause:short] Same energy. Same optimism.
(deadpan) Second, it's a shared joke. Nobody has to say "I'm working on self-control." {img:sarcastic_wow|2.5} They just say "NNN, bro," and suddenly it's a meme instead of a confession.
{sfx:bonk}{text:SOCIAL PROOF|slam} Third, a crowd gives you a scoreboard, and people tend to treat what strangers do as a hint about what's normal.
(whisper) [pause:beat] {text:THE PACKAGING|fade} The crowd is the product. The challenge is just the packaging.

## SCENE 06: Why Streaks Backfire
image: s06_snapped_chain
prompt: Doug holds a long fragile paper chain made of linked doodle days that has snapped in the middle, a small doodle storm cloud hovering overhead, and calmly picks up both loose ends. Plain white background, 16:9.

### Narration
(deadpan) {cam:zoom_out|6} Now, the streak. One popular explanation for why streaks feel powerful is {text:LOSS AVERSION|pop} loss aversion. Losing something tends to feel worse than gaining the same thing feels good.
(flat) So a streak turns every day into a tiny bet. [pause:short] Keep the chain, or lose the chain.
(smug) {sfx:record_scratch}{cam:shake} Here's the problem. Break the chain once, and some people decide the whole thing is ruined.
(deadpan) Psychologists call it the abstinence violation effect. One slip turns into a shrug, then a spiral. [pause] {text:SHAME SPIRAL|slam} That's the shame spiral.
(dramatic) {img:sarcastic_wow|2.5} It isn't a character flaw. It's a design flaw. The chain was {sfx:brick_crack} built to snap.
(deadpan) Here's a number that helps.
Researchers tracking people building everyday habits reported a median of {text:66 DAYS|slam} sixty-six days to feel automatic, with a range from eighteen to two hundred fifty-four.
(smug) {text:ONE MISS|pop} And in that same study, one missed day didn't seem to derail things.
[pause:beat] {sfx:triumphant_sting} One missed day is a blip. Blips are not verdicts.
(deadpan) Also, a {text:SMALL EXPERIMENT|jitter} small experiment with dieters found that kindness after a slip led to less overeating afterward.
(flat) {sfx:aww_chime} It was about dieting, not the challenge, so treat it as a hint.
{cam:pan_left|6} So, here's how to use a streak without the spiral.
(deadpan) [pause] {text:ROLLING WEEK|pop} Tip one. Track days per week, not an unbroken chain. Six out of seven is still a good week.
{text:IF THEN PLAN|slam} Tip two. Make an if-then plan for slips. If I slip, then I restart today, no speech required.
(smug) {text:DATA NOT VERDICT|fade} Tip three. Treat a slip as data, not a verdict. Data says, "what happened before that?" Verdicts say, "you're doomed."
